newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania's Romtelecom should be privatised-ministry.
newsitem.headline: Romania's Romtelecom should be privatised-ministry.

text.p: Romania's Communications Ministry said on Friday the state-run Romtelecom RA telephone company should become a joint venture with help from a strategic investor and then privatised.

"Privatisation of Romtelecom is a must, there is no doubt about it," ministry adviser Ion Matei told Reuters. "It's a process which could easily attract up to $4.0 billion, one of the biggest businesses in Romania."
His remarks were in response to reports in local media quoting communications minister Sorin Pantis as saying privatisation of Romtelecom would be high on his agenda.
Pantis took office on Thursday as part of a reformist government a month after ex-communists lost elections.

Romania's privatisation programme, launched in 1995 after long delays, has so far failed to deal with large utilities, including Romtelecom, which form the core of the economy and offer the best hope of attracting big foreign investment.

Matei said a restructuring and privatisation plan for Romtelecom submitted by ministry experts to the ousted leftist government last year had been rejected on grounds that "we don't sell out our country".

"It's ridiculous. Other East Europeans countries are well ahead with the privatisation process of their telecoms firms with help from foreign partners," he said. "We have to act now, otherwise it will be too late."
Under the plan, Romtelecom was expected to turn into a joint-stock company with help from a strategic investor.
"The investor should bring not only cash but managerial experience too," Matei said, adding that additional funds to develop the joint venture would come from share sales.

"There are several options to consider in the process," Matei added. "The state could either hold a majority in such a joint venture or keep so-called golden shares which could give it the right to veto. Clear agreements could allay fears that Romania might lose its communications sector."
Failure to tackle privatisation in communications might jeopardise financial assistance granted to Romania by international lenders to upgrade the sector, Matei said.

In 1993, the European Investment Bank (EIB) granted the government an 80 million ECU ($100 million) loan to modernise and expand the telecommunications system. In 1992 the EBRD extended Romtelecom a credit of 142 million ECUs to instal a fibre optic telecommunications network.
Part of the EIB loan was used to build 30 new telephone exchanges and modernise existing ones.

"The EBRD, for instance, made very clear that any future loans given to us will be commercial credits," Matei said. -- Adrian Dascalu, Bucharest Newsroom 40-1 31202634 ($ = 0.800 European Currency Unit ECUs)
